entry: City, prefecture of the Haute-Vienne department in west-central [[France]]. It was the administrative capital of the former Limousin region. The Roman city of Augustoritum was founded around 10 BC as part of the reorganization of the province by the emperor [[Augustus]]. During the [[Middle Ages]], the Abbey of Saint-Martial shaped the city, and its enamels were exported across the Christian world from the 12th century. [[Porcelain]] production, based on local kaolin deposits, became a major industry. The urban area had 323,494 inhabitants in 2022. Limoges joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2017 for crafts and popular arts.

Cyclic monoterpene, the main component of the essential oil of citrus peels. Its name comes from the Italian *limone*, "lemon". The (+)-isomer, d-limonene, is the form found in [[Citrus|citrus]] peel and is used as a food flavoring and as a solvent in cleaning products. The (−)-isomer, l-limonene, has a piny, [[Turpentine|turpentine]]-like odor and occurs in caraway, dill and [[Bergamot orange]]. Limonene oxidizes easily in moist air and is a precursor to carvone.

Large, chauffeur-driven luxury car with a partition between the driver and passengers. The name derives from the French region of Limousin, though the link to the car is uncertain; one theory connects it to the [[Cloak|cloaks]] worn by local shepherds. A stretch limousine has a very long wheelbase. In some countries, including the United States, a limousine service may be any pre-booked hire car with a driver. The first U.S. president to ride in a car, William McKinley, did so in a steam Locomobile in 1899. U.S. limousine business declined after the [[Great Recession]] and the rise of ride-sharing apps.

River of southern Africa, rising in [[South Africa]] and flowing generally east through [[Mozambique]] to the [[Indian Ocean]]. It is about 1,750 km (1,090 mi) long and drains a basin of 415,000 sq km (160,000 sq mi). Its mean discharge at the mouth is 170 m³/s to 313 m³/s, the second-largest of any African river draining to the Indian Ocean, after the [[Zambezi]]. Vasco da Gama anchored off its mouth in 1498 and is credited as the first European to sight the river. The river forms much of the border between South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe. [[Rudyard Kipling]] called it the "great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River" in the *Just So Stories*. Rainfall is seasonal and unreliable, and heavy rain from a cyclone caused the catastrophic 2000 Mozambique flood in February 2000. Fossil sites in the Makapans Valley contain [[Australopithecus]] remains from 3.5 million years ago. About 14 million people live in the basin.

American songwriter, actor, filmmaker and librettist. He created the Broadway musicals *In the Heights* and *Hamilton*, and *Hamilton* won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and 11 Tony Awards. He wrote the soundtracks for the animated films *Moana*, *Vivo* and *Encanto*, and received two [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for songs from *Moana* and *Encanto*. He has won five [[Grammy Awards]]. Miranda made his directing debut with *Tick, Tick... Boom!* and has been politically active on behalf of [[Puerto Rico]], raising funds after Hurricane Maria in 2017.

Peruvian woman, the youngest confirmed mother in medical history. At the age of five years, seven months and 21 days, she gave birth by [[Caesarean section|caesarean section]] on May 14, 1939. Precocious puberty left her with mature reproductive organs; her menarche had occurred at eight months of age. Her pregnancy was confirmed by specialists in [[Lima]]. Her son, Gerardo, was raised believing she was his sister until he learned at age 10 that she was his mother. She has never revealed the identity of the father.

City (pop., 2020: 291,082), capital of [[Nebraska]], United States. Founded in 1856 as the village of Lancaster, it was renamed after [[Abraham Lincoln]] and became the state capital in 1869. Its state capitol, completed in 1932, is the nation's second-tallest. The University of Nebraska, founded in Lincoln in 1869, is the state's largest university. The U.S. Department of State designated the city "refugee-friendly" in the 1970s, and Vietnamese, Karen, Sudanese and Yazidi refugees have resettled there.

Canadian fashion model. She signed with Elite Model Management in 1984 and became the longtime muse of photographer Steven Meisel. Evangelista was one of the "Big 6" supermodels of the late 1980s and 1990s, alongside [[Naomi Campbell]], [[Kate Moss]] and [[Cindy Crawford]]. Described as the "chameleon" of the fashion industry, she is known for the remark "We don't wake up for less than $10,000 a day." She retired in 1998 and returned three years later, working only sporadically. In 2008, viewers of the television show *Fashion File* voted her "The Greatest Supermodel of All Time."

American actress. Before entering film, she was a stage actress praised for the title role in [[Bertolt Brecht|Brecht]]'s *Mother Courage and Her Children*. She made her film debut as Mrs. Oxheart in *Popeye* (1980). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing the male character Billy Kwan in *The Year of Living Dangerously*, making her the first person to win an Oscar for playing a character of the opposite sex. From 2009 to 2023 she played Henrietta "Hetty" Lange on the CBS series *NCIS: Los Angeles*. She also provided the narrator's voice for the [[God of War (franchise)|God of War]] video games.

American actress, star of the 1972 hardcore film [[Deep Throat (film)|Deep Throat]]. She later accused her husband, Chuck Traynor, of coercing her into making the film, an account she gave in her 1980 autobiography *Ordeal*. Some people involved in her films later described her as a willing participant. She became a born-again Christian and a spokeswoman for the feminist [[Pornography|anti-pornography]] movement. By 2001 she had distanced herself from anti-pornography activists, saying she had felt used for political purposes and had moderated her views on pornography.

American singer of rock, folk, pop, country and soul. She has earned 11 [[Grammy Awards]] and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2014. Her single "You're No Good" reached number one on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100, and she charted 38 singles on that chart in all. She lent her voice to over 120 albums, collaborating with [[Dolly Parton]], [[Frank Zappa]], [[Neil Young]] and [[Johnny Cash]]. She retired in 2011 and soon revealed that a degenerative condition, first diagnosed as [[Parkinson's disease]] and later identified as progressive supranuclear palsy, had left her unable to sing.

American actress and singer. As a child she appeared on [[Soap opera|soap operas]], and she became a teen star in the Walt Disney comedy *The Parent Trap* (1998), playing reunited identical twins. Her role as Cady Heron in *Mean Girls* (2004) affirmed her status as a teen idol. Her album *Speak* (2004) was certified platinum. Personal struggles, including legal issues and rehabilitation stints, plagued her career for nearly a decade from 2006. Later she starred in [[Netflix]] romantic comedies, including *Falling for Christmas* (2022).

Unilineal descent group tracing its ancestry to a demonstrably shared ancestor, known as the apical ancestor. The word derives from Middle English *linage*, from Latin *linea* ("line"). Lineages differ from [[Clan|clans]], which may lack a documented apical ancestor. Three forms are recognized: matrilineal, in which descent runs through the mother, as among the Minangkabau of [[Indonesia]] and the Khasi of [[India]]; patrilineal, which is more common globally and is found across much of [[Southeast Asia]]; and ambilineal, in which individuals choose their mother's or father's group, common in modern societies such as the [[United States]] and [[Western Europe]]. In bilineal, or double, descent, members belong to both lines, as among the Yako of [[Nigeria]]. Lineages shape [[Inheritance|inheritance]] of property and titles, often have religious significance, and provide stability and reciprocal obligations.

Equation in the form a₁x₁ + … + aₙxₙ + b = 0, with unknowns x₁,…,xₙ and coefficients that are not all zero. With one variable, it has exactly one solution. With two variables, its solutions form a [[Line (geometry)|line]] in the [[Euclidean plane]], which is the origin of the term "linear"; with n variables they form a hyperplane in [[Euclidean space]]. Linear equations are central to mathematics, [[Physics|physics]] and [[Engineering|engineering]], partly because nonlinear systems are often well approximated by linear ones. Coefficients are usually [[Real number|real numbers]], but the theory applies to any [[Field (mathematics)|field]].

Method for optimizing a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints. The feasible region is a convex polytope, and a linear programming [[Algorithm|algorithm]] finds the point in it where the objective function is largest or smallest. It is a special case of [[Mathematical optimization|mathematical optimization]]. It is widely used in mathematics and, to a lesser extent, in business, [[Economics|economics]] and engineering, with applications in transportation, energy, telecommunications and manufacturing. Systems of linear inequalities were studied by Fourier, who published a solution method in 1827. Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief explored its applications in the late 1930s, and it became prominent during World War II. From 1946 to 1947, George B. Dantzig independently developed the general formulation for U.S. Air Force planning. Kantorovich and T. C. Koopmans shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

Statistical method for modeling the relationship between a scalar response (dependent variable) and one or more explanatory variables as a linear combination. Simple linear regression has one explanatory variable; multiple linear regression has two or more. It is usually fitted by [[Least squares|least squares]], which [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] published in 1805, although [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] claimed to have invented it earlier. Because squared errors give outliers excessive weight, robust cost functions are preferred for datasets with many outliers. Linear regression is also a supervised [[Machine learning|machine learning]] algorithm.

Textile made from the bast fibers of the [[Flax|flax]] plant. Linen is strong and absorbent and dries faster than [[Cotton|cotton]], which makes it comfortable in hot weather. It tends to wrinkle and takes longer to harvest and process than cotton. Dyed flax fibers found in a cave in present-day [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] suggest that woven fabric from wild flax may date back over 30,000 years. In ancient [[Mesopotamia]], linen was used mainly by wealthy people, such as priests, and in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] it was used for mummy wrappings, burial shrouds and daily clothing. Linen is mentioned in the [[Bible]]. The word is related to Latin *linum*, the name of the flax plant, and the word [[Line (geometry)|line]] comes from the use of linen thread to determine a straight line.

Language used for communication between groups that do not share a native language. The term derives from the medieval Mediterranean *Lingua Franca*, a Romance-based pidgin used by traders from the 11th to the 19th centuries; Western Europeans were called "Franks" by [[Levant|Levantine]] peoples. Lingua francas have arisen for commercial, religious, diplomatic and administrative purposes. Some are established languages, such as [[Aramaic]] in the ancient empires or [[Arabic]] in the caliphates, while others are pidgins or [[Creole language|creoles]]. English is now the preeminent international lingua franca, underpinning [[Aviation|aviation]] protocols and science.

Branch of [[Anthropology|anthropology]] concerned with how language influences social life. It originated in efforts to document [[Endangered language|endangered languages]], especially indigenous languages of North America, and it examines how language shapes [[Communication|communication]], [[Identity (social science)|social identity]] and group membership, and large-scale cultural beliefs and ideologies. It emerged from three paradigms. The first, anthropological linguistics, documents languages and their structure. The second, which Dell Hymes preferred to call linguistic anthropology, studies language use in context, with the speech event as its unit of analysis; Hymes also criticized the cognitive emphasis of [[Noam Chomsky]], arguing for an ethnographic focus on language in use. The third, begun in the late 1980s, uses linguistic tools to study anthropological questions such as identity, shared ideologies and narrative.

Branch of [[Linguistics|linguistics]] concerned with classifying languages by their structural features so that they can be compared. Its aim is to describe and explain the structural diversity and common properties of the world's languages. Subdisciplines include phonological typology (sound features), syntactic typology (word order and form), lexical typology (vocabulary) and theoretical typology (universal tendencies). Unlike genealogical linguistics, typology groups languages by formal similarity rather than historical descent, and modern samples are drawn evenly from different language families. In the Middle Ages, [[Latin]] was the model language of linguistics. In 1818 August Wilhelm Schlegel classified languages as lacking grammatical structure, agglutinative or inflectional. Modern typology emerged in the 1960s: at a 1961 conference on language universals at Dobbs Ferry, Joseph Greenberg proposed 45 linguistic universals based on data from 30 languages.

American business and employment-oriented [[Social networking service|social networking service]] owned by [[Microsoft]]. It was launched on May 5, 2003, by Reid Hoffman and Eric Ly, and is used mainly for professional networking, job listings and career development. By early 2026 it had more than 1.3 billion registered members in over 200 countries and territories. Microsoft bought LinkedIn in December 2016 for $26.2 billion, its largest acquisition at the time. [[Russia]] banned it in 2016, [[Kazakhstan]] in 2021 and [[China]] in 2023.

American rock band formed in Agoura Hills, California, in 1996. Categorized as [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] and [[Nu metal|nu metal]], its early music fused heavy metal and hip-hop. The debut album *Hybrid Theory* (2000) was certified Diamond by the Recording Industry Association of America, and its singles included "In the End" and "Crawling". The band has sold over 100 million records worldwide and won two [[Grammy Awards]]. After the suicide of lead vocalist Chester Bennington in July 2017, the band went on hiatus; it reformed in 2024 with vocalist Emily Armstrong and released the album *From Zero*.

American chemist and peace activist. He won the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry in 1954 for his work on the chemical bond, and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is the only person to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes. He helped found [[Quantum chemistry|quantum chemistry]] and [[Molecular biology|molecular biology]], introducing orbital hybridization and the first accurate scale of electronegativities. He showed the importance of the alpha helix and beta sheet in protein structure, and his work inspired the work of [[James Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]] on the structure of DNA. In later years he promoted nuclear disarmament, orthomolecular medicine and dietary supplements, especially [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]]; none of his ideas on large vitamin doses has gained much acceptance in mainstream science.

Finnish-American software engineer, creator and lead developer of the [[Linux]] kernel since 1991. He also created the distributed version control system Git. The first Linux prototypes were publicly released in late 1991, and Version 1.0 followed on March 14, 1994. He switched the kernel's license from one that forbade commercial use to the GNU General Public License version 2. Torvalds worked for Transmeta in California from 1997 to 2003. He was named equally for [[Linus Pauling|the chemist Linus Pauling]] and the Peanuts cartoon character Linus, he has said. He received the 2012 Millennium Technology Prize.

Family of free and [[Open source|open-source]] [[Unix]]-like [[Operating system|operating systems]] built on the [[Kernel (operating system)|Linux kernel]]. The kernel was first released on September 17, 1991, by [[Linus Torvalds]]. Distributions such as [[Debian]], Fedora Linux, Linux Mint, Arch Linux and Ubuntu combine the kernel with GNU and other third-party software to form complete systems; commercial distributions include Red Hat Enterprise Linux. Linux was originally designed as a clone of Unix and is distributed under the GNU General Public License. Originally developed for x86-based [[Personal computer|personal computers]], it has been ported to more platforms than any other operating system. Together with [[Android (operating system)|Android]], which uses a Linux-based kernel, it has the largest installed base of general-purpose operating systems. As of March 2024 it was used by around 4 percent of desktop computers.
